blocks.text: Write a clear, concise summary of the project here. In two to three paragraphs, explain what the project is, what it produces, and who it is for. This is the elevator pitch — assume the reader is technically literate but unfamiliar with your specific domain.

You can expand slightly on the context: where did this project fit in a larger research programme or engineering effort? Was it solo or collaborative? Is it a finished product or an ongoing investigation?

Describe the gap or problem that motivated this work. What existed before? Why was it insufficient? A well-written motivation section makes the reader feel the urgency of the problem before you present your solution.
The best way to capture something meaningful about a system is often through the places where it breaks.

items: Existing methods rely on fully-labelled datasets that are expensive to obtain.

blocks.text: Describe your high-level strategy before diving into implementation. What framework or methodology did you choose, and why? What alternatives did you consider and rule out?

items.title: Data Collection & Preprocessing
items.text: Describe your data sources, how you curated them, any cleaning or normalisation steps, and how you handled edge cases or class imbalance.

items.title: Model Architecture
items.text: Describe the model family you chose, key design decisions (e.g. attention heads, hidden dimensions), and any modifications to standard architectures.

items.title: Training & Evaluation
items.text: Describe your training loop, hyperparameter choices, loss function, and how you measured success. What metrics did you optimise for and why?

items.title: Deployment
items.text: Describe how the model or system was packaged and served — API, CLI tool, notebook, or other interface.

blocks.text: Present your quantitative and qualitative findings. Be specific: include numbers, comparisons to baselines, and confidence intervals or standard deviations where appropriate.

blocks.title: Notable qualitative findings
items: The model generalises well to out-of-distribution samples in three of the four tested subdomains.
Failure cases are concentrated in examples with ambiguous label boundaries — a known challenge in this task.
Inference speed improvements stem primarily from a fused attention kernel, not architectural changes.

blocks.text: Honest reflection on what went wrong, what took longer than expected, and what you would do differently. This section builds credibility — it shows you understand the limitations of your own work.

items.title: Data sparsity in rare categories
items.text: Describe the problem in one sentence. Then describe how you addressed or worked around it.

items.text: Describe the problem and the mitigation strategy — e.g. gradient clipping, learning rate warmup, layer-wise decay.

items.title: Deployment latency under concurrent load
items.text: Describe any infrastructure or batching strategies you used to resolve the issue in production.
